title: The Quizmaster Advantage
text:
In 1977 Lee Ross, Teresa Amabile and Julia Steinmetz of Stanford University staged a quiz game. Pairs of students drew cards to decide their roles at random. One became the questioner, the other the contestant.

The questioner was asked to write ten challenging but fair general knowledge questions, drawing on any area they knew well, from a favorite book to their hobbies. The questioner then asked the contestant these questions aloud. Since each questioner could choose obscure topics they personally knew, contestants missed many of the answers.

Afterward, both participants rated the general knowledge of the questioner and of the contestant. Contestants rated questioners as far more knowledgeable than themselves. Observers who watched the game reached the same conclusion. Questioners, however, did not rate themselves as superior. Everyone knew the roles had been assigned by chance and that questioners had the huge advantage of choosing the questions, yet the contestants and observers still concluded that the person asking the questions was simply smarter.

The study showed how easily we mistake the advantages of a social role for qualities of the person who holds it, whether in a quiz, a job interview, or a meeting where one person sets the agenda.
lesson: The person asking the questions, setting the agenda or holding the title often seems smarter than they are. Judge people by what they know, not by the position they speak from.
people: Lee Ross, Teresa Amabile, Julia Steinmetz
source: Ross, L., Amabile, T. M., and Steinmetz, J. L. (1977). Social roles, social control, and biases in social-perception processes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 35(7), 485-494.
